transcript:
[Header]
Date: 2025-05-14
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Laura Chen (Redwood SE), Markus Lee (AstraHealth CTO), Priya Nair (ML Eng), Daniel Ramos (Infra)

[Summary]
(automated) Technical deep dive: autoscaling behavior, burst policies, queueing, reserved GPUs, and tradeoffs around batching/KV cache/quantization for low-latency EHR summarization.

[Topics]
- Autoscaling policies (scale-to-zero vs reserved + burst)
- Queueing models and tail latency
- Reserved GPU sizing and bin-packing
- KV cache warmup and shared caches across instances
- Batching and micro-batching for mixed workloads
- Quantization impact on throughput/latency
- VPC/on-prem constraints (network, KMS, audit logs)

[Transcript]
[00:00] Samir Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — Samir here, Laura from infra is with me. You all good on audio?
[00:07] Markus Lee: Yeah, hi Samir, hi Laura. Markus here.
[00:09] Priya Nair: Priya on the call.
[00:11] Daniel Ramos: Daniel, infra.
[00:15] Laura Chen: Cool, so agenda for today is to dig into autoscaling and capacity planning for your EHR summarization flows. We'll talk about reserved capacity, burst policies, queueing behaviour, and then recommendations for batching and quantization. Sound right?
[00:28] Markus Lee: Yep, that's great. Our main concerns are 95/99 latency SLOs and predictable cost. Last time we saw big spikes during peak clinic hours and the fallback to smaller models increased error rates.
[00:42] Samir Patel: Understood. Can you remind us of your traffic shape? Priya, you said you'd share a 7 day trace? What's the typical qps and peak bursts?
[00:51] Priya Nair: Yeah, typical steady state is about 25 qps, peaks up to 250 qps for 10-15 minutes in the morning window. Long-tail requests when clinicians do batch uploads; those can be heavier, like longer sequence length, more tokens.
[01:08] Daniel Ramos: Also note we are VPC-only for PII, and we need KMS integration for key rotation. Any private deploy notes there?
[01:16] Laura Chen: VPC on Redwood Private is supported; we map the private control plane, and KMS/HSM via customer-managed keys. There are some networking RTTs to account for with on-prem though — we can run a latency baseline. We'll call out network envelope in the sizing.
[01:28] Markus Lee: Perfect. Let's jump into autoscaling models — reserved GPUs + burst vs pure scale-to-zero.
[01:34] Samir Patel: Sure. For workloads like yours with predictable daily peaks we generally recommend a reserved pool sized to cover 50-70% of expected peak QPS, then a burst policy that spins up extra instances. The reason is cold-starts and KV cache warmup: a warm pool reduces tail latency.
[01:51] Laura Chen: To add, Redwood's runtime supports instant warm pools for KV cache if instances are kept alive; when you scale from zero you lose the KV cache which causes heavy latency at first token, especially for long contexts. So scale-to-zero saves cost but incurs a tail-latency penalty on bursts.
[02:12] Markus Lee: How long does KV cache warmup typically take if we spin new GPUs for a model like longformer-ish — say 8k tokens?
[02:20] Laura Chen: It depends on batch sizes and request distribution. Rough ballpark: initial generation for a single request might be fine after model load, but priming the KV cache for prefix reuse often takes multiple requests. For 8k contexts, you can see 1-2 minutes of elevated per-token latency as cache warms. If you have many small requests with shared prefixes, caches warm faster.
[02:44] Priya Nair: What's the tradeoff if we enable KV cache sharing across instances? Are there consistency or security concerns?
[02:51] Laura Chen: You can use a shared KV cache within a cluster; it's faster for warmups but adds network overhead and complexity. In VPC/private deployments we ensure traffic stays on the private network, and we can enable encryption in transit. There's extra operational complexity and potential contention on the cache store — so it's a balance.
[03:10] Daniel Ramos: For reserved GPUs, what sizing do you recommend for 25 steady qps and 250 peak? Also model is a 7B quantized variant.
[03:18] Laura Chen: For a 7B quantized model on A100-like hardware, rough throughput numbers: single GPU can handle ~100-150 small-chat qps with micro-batching optimized — but that drops with longer contexts. Given 25 steady and 250 peaks, we'd recommend reserving 2 GPUs to cover steady and small buffer, and allow autoscale to add up to 4-6 GPUs for bursts. We'll test with your trace to produce precise numbers.
[03:44] Samir Patel: Right — and with intelligent queuing, we can keep tail latency bounded. Our recommended queueing model is token-aware headroom: maintain a small request queue up to N ms and prefer lightweight fallbacks rather than unbounded queuing.
[03:59] Markus Lee: Token-aware headroom? Can you explain that a bit more?
[04:02] Laura Chen: Sure. Instead of pure FIFO, we prioritize requests based on expected token cost + SLA deadline. So a short 30-token request that needs a 200ms tail window gets scheduled ahead of a 2k-token long-run that would block others. This reduces P95/P99 for interactive workloads.
[04:21] Priya Nair: Interesting — what about batching? We worry that batching can hurt latency if it waits to aggregate.
[04:27] Laura Chen: We do continuous batching: the runtime collects requests for a very small window (2-8ms) and then dispatches. For mixed workloads we use adaptive batch sizing — small batches for low-latency, larger ones for throughputy offline requests. There's an operating point you can tune per route.
[04:44] Daniel Ramos: Any recommended policies for when a queued request should be rejected or sent to fallback models? Our clinicians prefer results rather than errors but would accept lower-quality fallback.
[04:53] Samir Patel: We usually configure two-level fallback: first, a quantized, smaller model as an automatic fallback for heavy tail; second, a degraded-mode summary (e.g., template-based) as last resort. These fallbacks are policy-driven and you can set thresholds by latency or queue depth.
[05:10] Markus Lee: Quick question on quantization. We currently use 4-bit quantized weights; how much CPU/GPU throughput improvement vs latency tradeoffs are typical?
[05:18] Laura Chen: 4-bit quantization often improves throughput 1.5x–2.5x depending on op fusion and kernels; latency per-token can be slightly higher or similar depending on kernel optimizations. The main thing is accuracy regressions — some prompts may degrade. We recommend running eval sets to ensure quality is acceptable before rolling to production.
[05:37] Priya Nair: On the note of evals, can Redwood run end-to-end regression tests as part of the pilot?
[05:42] Samir Patel: Yes, we'll include an eval harness and can tie regression alerts to rollbacks. We'll also provide a recommended quantization profile per model.
[05:50] Laura Chen: Back to scaling: one pattern that works well is a hybrid policy — reserved pool sized for median+buffer, aggressive burst autoscaling with pre-warming heuristics, and a short ingress queue with SLA-based drop/fallback.
[06:05] Markus Lee: Pre-warming heuristics — is that a warm-up replica that spins at the edge of being active so it's fast to serve?
[06:12] Laura Chen: Exactly. We keep a minimal footprint of warm instances that have the model and KV cache partially primed. When a burst is predicted (e.g., cron-scheduled or detection via traffic spike detectors), we spin additional nodes and route new traffic into the warm pool to minimize tail.
[06:26] Daniel Ramos: How do you predict bursts? We have scheduled peaks but sometimes weird ad-hoc events cause traffic.
[06:33] Laura Chen: We have both scheduled rules and adaptive signals using short-term traffic trend detection. For unpredictable spikes, the autoscaler looks at rate-of-change and ramps quickly with a short cool-down to avoid thrashing.
[06:44] Priya Nair: Any concerns about multi-tenancy and noisy neighbor with reserved GPUs in Dedicated?
[06:51] Samir Patel: For Dedicated we carve pools per customer, so noisy neighbor isn't an issue across customers. Within a customer's pool if you have mixed workloads we recommend isolating critical low-latency routes to separate GPU groups or using QoS slots.
[07:04] Markus Lee: Can you walk through an example queueing model math for 95/99 with 250 qps peaks and average service time per request of, say, 120ms?
[07:15] Laura Chen: Sure — rough Erlang-style approximation: with service time 120ms you need concurrency = qps * service_time = 250 * 0.12 = 30 effective threads. If each GPU supports concurrency of ~8-12 depending on batch, you'd target ~3-4 GPUs to handle concurrency headroom, but you also need headroom for variance and tail so bump to 4-6 GPUs. The queue should be sized to hold short bursts, but anything beyond the cold-start threshold should trigger scale-out or fallback.
[07:48] Priya Nair: That math helps. We'll send actual service time distributions.
[07:52] Samir Patel: Great. A couple of operational notes: we recommend synthetic load tests that mimic token length distributions — not just qps. Long sequences consume KV and increase per-request time.
[08:02] Markus Lee: On the networking side, for Private deploy, what added latency should we account for compared to hosted?
[08:08] Laura Chen: Depends on cross-region hops and how your VPC is set up. Typical added RTT might be 5-40ms depending on peering. Also KMS calls for encryption can add tens of ms on cold key usage; we recommend key caching strategies.
[08:24] Daniel Ramos: Thoughts on rack-level vs zone-level placement for Reserved GPUs? We have AWS placements across two AZs.
[08:31] Laura Chen: For high availability pick multi-AZ replicas; for low P99 prefer single-zone hot pool plus cross-zone cold pool as fallback to avoid cross-AZ latency on hot path. There's still tradeoffs in failover time.
[08:45] Priya Nair: Any simple heuristics for reserved capacity percent? You said 50-70% earlier; is 60% a safe starting point?
[08:51] Samir Patel: 60% is a good conservative starting point for predictable daily peaks. We'll refine after running the 48-hour benchmark using your trace.
[08:59] Markus Lee: Let's talk about billing and cost controls — if we keep a large reserved pool costs go up. Any suggestions for dynamic policies to reclaim idle GPUs overnight?
[09:08] Laura Chen: Configure scheduled scale-down windows overnight and allow scale-to-zero for non-critical routes. For critical routes, use smaller reserved pools and rely on burst policies. Redwood Console also gives token-level cost attribution so you can find expensive prompts.
[09:20] Daniel Ramos: On the subject of emergency scale, how fast can Redwood spin up another GPU in Dedicated vs Private?
[09:27] Samir Patel: For Dedicated hosted capacity, spinning new containers with pre-provisioned GPUs is a matter of seconds to a minute depending on model load. For Private/on-prem it's limited by customer infra — if GPUs are already provisioned we can start containers quickly; if additional machines need provisioning it's longer (minutes to hours).
[09:46] Priya Nair: Regarding benchmarking, what's your recommended harness? We need to simulate mixed qps with long-tail token distributions.
[09:52] Laura Chen: We'll share our benchmark harness which supports request traces, token-length distributions, and can replay with configurable arrival processes (Poisson, Pareto bursts). We'll also run end-to-end latency and tail metrics and produce sizing recommendations.
[10:07] Markus Lee: Perfect. Can you also include KV cache priming tests in the benchmark so we can see warm vs cold metrics?
[10:12] Laura Chen: Yep — we'll produce both warm and cold run reports.
[10:16] Samir Patel: Quick note on model fallback: if your fallback model is on different GPUs or quantified more aggressively, be explicit about fallbacks in the routes and the console will surface failover counts.
[10:27] Markus Lee: Good, last thing — compliance: we need audit logs, per-token retention policies, and SOC2 scope. How does Redwood handle this with Private?
[10:36] Samir Patel: Private supports audit logging to your SIEM and configurable retention. We can scope SOC 2 controls in the enterprise package; I'll share the security pack after the call.
[10:46] Priya Nair: Sounds good. A couple of follow ups: can Laura provide a draft autoscale policy we'll test? Also, Samir to send pricing delta for reserved vs on-demand burst?
[10:55] Laura Chen: I'll draft the autoscale policy and include example parameters — target CPU/GPU utilization, cooldown windows, queue thresholds, and pre-warm sizes.
[11:03] Samir Patel: I'll include cost estimates for reserved 2/4/6 GPU combos and the blended cost under expected traffic. We'll attach the model-level quantization recommendations too.
[11:12] Markus Lee: Anything else on the tech side? If not, let's recap next steps.
[11:18] Daniel Ramos: No other technical Qs from me.
[11:20] Priya Nair: All good.
[11:22] Samir Patel: Recap: Redwood sends benchmark plan + harness by 2025-05-16, AstraHealth provides 7-day anonymized trace and SLOs by same date, Redwood to run a 48-hour pilot and return sizing recommendations and autoscale policy draft by 2025-05-19. Pilot kickoff week of 2025-05-26. Everyone ok?
[11:38] Markus Lee: Sounds good.
[11:40] Samir Patel: Great, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the docs and links. End call.

[End of transcript]
